title: Event queues and dispatch
lead: Build a FIFO dispatcher with deferred callbacks instead of recursive dispatch.
why: A handler can generate another action: adding a task may require refreshing a list. Immediately invoking another handler increases stack depth and can expose partially updated state. A queue stores the new event until a later dispatch step. This changes when processing occurs, so ordering must be specified as a contract rather than treated as an implementation detail.
objectives: Explain the difference between front and pop.
Complete the queue and callback in the starter.
Add an event log and verify FIFO.
prerequisites: Modules 1–5: functions, STL, ownership, testing and multi-file builds.

concepts.definition: The earliest enqueued item is processed first.
A callable supplied for execution at a later point.
How a lambda obtains access to surrounding values.
A function wrapper that contains no callable target.
Entering an operation before its previous invocation finishes.
Restricting incoming work when processing capacity is insufficient.
A condition preserved at the boundaries of permitted model operations.
An agreed observation by which a client distinguishes contract satisfaction from a defect.

sections.title: Why a queue is needed
paragraphs: A handler can generate another action: adding a task may require refreshing a list. Immediately invoking another handler increases stack depth and can expose partially updated state. A queue stores the new event until a later dispatch step. This changes when processing occurs, so ordering must be specified as a contract rather than treated as an implementation detail.

For input 3, 2, 3, the laboratory first enqueues all three numbers. Each three appends a one to the back. Processing therefore visits 3, 2, 3, 1, 1: total ten and five calls. Recursive dispatch would process a one immediately after the first three. Equal final totals do not prove equal behaviour; an event log can distinguish the implementations.

sections.title: FIFO operations
paragraphs: std::queue supplies push, front, pop, empty and size. front accesses the first element; pop removes it and returns nothing. Check empty before accessing front. The dispatcher copies the value into a local variable, removes the queued element and only then calls user code. A reference to the removed element is invalid after pop.

Removing the element before the callback means the current event is no longer counted as pending. The callback may append events after those already waiting. A queue has no arbitrary indexing or sorting operation: priority scheduling requires a different contract and structure. This exercise preserves arrival order, including repeated values that represent separate events.

sections.title: Functions as values
paragraphs: std::function<void(int)> stores a callable object such as a function or compatible lambda. void specifies no returned value and int specifies one event argument. Capturing [&total] accesses the original variable rather than copying it. total must outlive the callback. Here both belong to main and dispatch completes before the function returns.

An empty std::function contains no handler. The if(handler) condition checks whether a callable exists; it does not execute it. handler(event) is a separate invocation. Skipping an absent handler is this example’s policy, while another application might treat it as a diagnostic error. Do not invoke an empty callback or silently discard events without specifying the expected behaviour.

sections.title: Reentrancy and handler changes
paragraphs: Reentrancy occurs when a handler re-enters dispatch before the previous dispatch has finished. It does not require threads: everything can happen on one thread’s call stack. Queuing and refusing nested drain calls simplify reasoning. Finish the current command and restore its invariants before selecting the next event.

If a callback changes subscriber storage, traversal must not continue through an invalidated iterator. A later lesson snapshots subscriber identifiers and checks each subscription before invoking it. This laboratory has one callback that is not replaced during invocation. The restricted example deliberately separates FIFO reasoning from the more complex problem of managing callback lifetime.

sections.title: Bounds and termination
paragraphs: Input contains at most twelve numbers in 0…9. Only a three generates a one, and a one generates nothing. Each original event therefore causes at most one extra invocation, giving a maximum of twenty-four. This proves termination for the specified rule; it is not a general property of every event-driven system.

Replacing the generated one with another three prevents the queue from emptying. Predict that outcome before experimenting and propose a safe processing limit and overflow message. Real applications distinguish queue capacity, the budget for one dispatch step and rejection policy. A single timeout that kills the application and loses unfinished work does not replace those separate decisions.

sections.title: Testing more than the total
paragraphs: Compare inputs containing no threes, one three, only threes and an empty queue. Record processed separately from total. To verify FIFO, add a diagnostic trace in a separate stream or change output deliberately in a project copy. Do not claim the order is established merely because addition is commutative and the final total matches.

For independent transfer, design a notification queue with a capacity and an enqueue result. Specify whether a full buffer rejects input, merges equivalent refresh requests or evicts an item. Choose one policy for the exercise, explain it to the user and provide a trace whose observable result would differ under another policy.

sections.title: Laboratory contract: input to observation
paragraphs: Read n=0…12 followed by n values in 0…9. Fill FIFO before dispatch. Each handler adds its value to total; a three appends a one. Print total and processed. Invalid syntax, range or trailing tokens produce invalid.

Trace the first reference scenario before running. Exact stdin: "3 3 2 3". Expected stdout: "total 10 processed 5\n" Relate each algorithm step to state changes, distinguishing rejection from the point where a change is committed.

sections.title: Reading a working example
paragraphs: push places two before five. front is copied and pop removes the element. The empty queue ends the loop after two iterations. First identify data, ownership and the observable outcome. Then change exactly one initial condition and predict which observation changes. This connects syntax to a contract rather than memorizing finished source text.

The lambda captures total by reference. The first invocation adds seven. After handler={} the check is false and no call occurs. Compare the second example with the first: what new boundary is covered, and which test distinguishes the correct implementation from a superficially similar mistake? Retain both sources, predictions and actual observations so that the explanation can be reproduced.

readinessCheck.question: What is required when an operation with a strong guarantee fails?
readinessCheck.explanation: The guarantee concerns the specified model at an operation boundary.

readinessCheck.question: Who owns an object supplied through an ordinary reference?
answers: Ownership is specified separately; a reference does not transfer it.
readinessCheck.explanation: The owner must outlive use of the reference.

readinessCheck.question: How is a driver with its own main built?
answers: Instead of application main, sharing model sources.
readinessCheck.explanation: The application and driver have separate entry points and builds.
